scenario.prompt_to_agent:
pc2 (200.1.1.2) lost all connectivity to the partner network, and
the partner reports pc1 (195.11.14.2) cannot reach pc2 either.
Our NOC tried to inspect router2 but vtysh commands on it error
out entirely -- they cannot even display the routing table. pc2
can still ping router2's address 200.1.1.1. Find what broke.

injection.action: kill the entire FRR stack (watchdog, zebra and bgpd) on router2
injection.command: pkill -9 watchfrr; pkill -9 zebra; pkill -9 bgpd

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 FRR routing stack (zebra + bgpd,
  watchfrr included)
Mechanism: the whole FRR service on router2 is dead -- not just
  one daemon. With bgpd gone the eBGP session's TCP connection
  closes, so router1 immediately drops the session and withdraws
  200.1.1.0/24; pc1's traffic toward pc2 then dies at router1 with
  no route, and pc2's replies/pings toward 195.11.14.0/24 have no
  usable end-to-end path either. With zebra ALSO dead, vtysh has
  no daemon left to attach to, so it fails outright -- unlike a
  bgpd-only crash, where vtysh stays responsive via zebra. (A
  stale kernel route to 195.11.14.0/24 may linger on router2,
  since zebra died without cleaning up; end-to-end traffic still
  fails because router1 has withdrawn 200.1.1.0/24.) router2's
  kernel itself is alive: it still answers on its connected
  addresses, e.g. pc2 -> 200.1.1.1.
Localization: router2
Root cause: FRR routing stack (zebra and bgpd) not running on
  router2
Fix: restart FRR on router2 (`service frr restart`)
scenario.fix_spec:
Restart the FRR service on router2 (`service frr restart`). This brings back
watchfrr, zebra and bgpd from /etc/frr/frr.conf; the eBGP session to router1
re-establishes, the inter-AS prefixes are re-exchanged, and pc1 reaches pc2
normally. router1 needs no change.
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: FRR routing stack (zebra and bgpd) not running on router2
must-distinguish-scope: recognizes the whole FRR service is down (vtysh unreachable), not just a single daemon, a link failure, or a config change
bonus-notes-kernel-alive: notes router2 still answers on its connected addresses (kernel/data plane alive); only the routing control plane died

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: the FRRouting (FRR) routing stack (zebra/bgpd) on both routers is down. With BGP not running, dynamic routes between the two LANs are not exchanged.

Mechanism: When bgpd/zebra stop, router1 retains only its directly connected networks. As a result, traffic from pc1 (195.11.14.2) toward pc2’s subnet (200.1.1.0/24) hits router1 (195.11.14.1), which has no route and returns ICMP Destination Net Unreachable—exactly what we observe when pinging pc2 from pc1. pc2 can still reach its default gateway (router2: 200.1.1.1) because that is local L2/L3. Router2’s kernel still shows a leftover “proto bgp” route to 195.11.14.0/24 via 193.10.11.1, creating asymmetric reachability that cannot complete without a return path via router1.

Localization: 
- router1: ip route shows only connected routes (no 200.1.1.0/24), and systemctl reports frr.service inactive (dead).
- router2: systemctl also shows frr.service inactive (dead); NOC reports vtysh fails, consistent with FRR not running. Its kernel table oddly retains a BGP-learned route to 195.11.14.0/24.

Root cause: FRRouting service is stopped on both routers, bringing the eBGP session down and removing the 200.1.1.0/24 route from router1.

Corrective fix: Start and enable FRR on both routers (systemctl start frr; systemctl enable frr), verify BGP peers establish (neighbor 193.10.11.1/193.10.11.2) and routes 195.11.14.0/24 and 200.1.1.0/24 appear on the opposite routers. Investigate why FRR was stopped (check /var/log/frr/frr.log, watchfrr) to prevent recurrence.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly identifies the entire FRR service as stopped (frr.service inactive) and notes vtysh inability to attach, distinguishing a full FRR outage from a single-daemon, link, or config issue.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly notes router2’s kernel/data-plane is up (pc2 can reach 200.1.1.1) and that FRR/vtysh is dead, matching the kernel-alive/control-plane-down observation.

Starting/enabling the FRR service (bringing zebra/bgpd back up) on the routers—specifically restarting FRR on router2 as the expected fix—will re-establish the eBGP session and restore the missing routes.

The agent's conclusion that FRR is not running and that loss of BGP routes explains the connectivity failures is well supported by the investigation log (systemctl outputs and ping failures). One claim (that router2's kernel retains a stale 'proto bgp' route) is asserted without explicit evidence in the log, but overall the chain of evidence-to-conclusion is coherent.
